description_full: Carpenter Technology Corporation manufactures, fabricates, and distributes specialty metals in the United States, Europe, the Asia Pacific, Mexico, Canada, and internationally. It operates in two segments, Specialty Alloys Operations and Performance Engineered Products. The company offers specialty alloys, including titanium alloys, powder metals, stainless steels, alloy steels, and tool steels, as well as metal powders and parts. It serves the aerospace, defense, medical, transportation, energy, industrial, and consumer markets. The company was founded in 1889 and is headquartered in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.

Stock-based compensation of $6K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 6× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (1/10).
financial_summary: Carpenter Technology Corporatio is a large-cap industrials business with a $14.4B market cap on $3.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.

Returns on capital run at 14% against a 10% cost of capital, a 3-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, and 17% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $362M in free cash flow — roughly 12 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.14× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.4× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 19× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 1.5%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 2.5% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 2.0× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 22% operating margin runs 14pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.02x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 17% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 44% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 53% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 49% and a beta of 1.22, it amplifies market moves.
Liquidity is deep, with about $287.3M traded a day, and interest is running hot at 1.6x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 70% in the 2020 crash, 42% in the 2022 bear market and 84% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $188 (margin of safety -55%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 70%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $127 to $281 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: EV/EBITDA 17.6 vs 13.4 and P/FCF 39.9 vs 22.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 18% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.5% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 7 covering analysts target $438 on average, 50% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 14% earns above the cost of capital of 10.3%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.07).
It runs a 17% gross margin and converts 12% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 1.14x.
ROE of 24% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 16pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 0.9% of revenue on R&D and 0.8% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.4x net debt to EBITDA ($393.3M of cash against $690.7M of debt), with interest covered 18.6x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 8.1, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.0% over 3 years, 16.2% over 5 years and 5.6% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 17%).
At current returns, reinvesting 49% of profits supports about 6.6% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 19.4% a year over five years.
Capex runs 1.6x depreciation (7.8% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.5%, and institutions hold 96%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (23 sales, net $54.6M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.5% (1.2% in buybacks and 0.3% in dividends).
The share count has grown 0.5% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 38 consecutive years, raising it 0.6% a year over the last five.
people: With about 4,500 employees, each generates about $694K of revenue, 1.9x the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 4.2% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $81K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.1M (6x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
